name: Security of Connected Medical Devices
title: Security of Connected Medical Devices
answer: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, imaging systems, and implantable devices, along with their supporting software, data flows, and cloud or hospital interfaces. It includes device authentication, encryption of patient data in transit and at rest, patch management, and segmentation from hospital networks. The scope also extends to supply chain components, legacy operating systems, and remote service access used by vendors. This area sits within governance and compliance because device security failures can affect patient safety and regulatory standing.

sections.body: Security of connected medical devices covers the protection of networked clinical hardware such as infusion pumps, patient monitors, imaging systems, and implantable devices, along with their supporting software, data flows, and cloud or hospital interfaces. It includes device authentication, encryption of patient data in transit and at rest, patch management, and segmentation from hospital networks. The scope also extends to supply chain components, legacy operating systems, and remote service access used by vendors. This area sits within governance and compliance because device security failures can affect patient safety and regulatory standing.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: These devices run on embedded controllers, real-time operating systems, and increasingly on general-purpose computing platforms with wireless radios such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth Low Energy, and proprietary medical telemetry. Many connect through hospital gateways, edge servers, or vendor cloud services that aggregate telemetry and push software updates. Security infrastructure includes network access control, device identity certificates, and isolated virtual LANs for clinical equipment. Some newer devices include hardware roots of trust and secure boot, but many deployed systems still rely on older, unpatchable operating systems.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Security work is done through a mix of premarket threat modeling, static and dynamic analysis of firmware, and postmarket monitoring of device behavior and network traffic. Teams inventory connected devices, map their data flows, and assess vulnerabilities against frameworks such as CVSS and manufacturer disclosure programs. Penetration testing often focuses on wireless interfaces, update mechanisms, and the boundary between device and hospital information systems. Because clinical uptime is critical, patching is usually scheduled around care workflows and may require vendor coordination or compensating controls.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk here center on patient safety, data privacy, and accountability when a compromised device causes harm. Regulations such as FDA premarket and postmarket guidance, EU MDR, and health data protection rules require manufacturers to document security risk management and provide coordinated vulnerability disclosure. Hospitals must balance clinical availability against security updates, and contracts often define who is responsible for patching, monitoring, and incident response. Provenance matters for software bills of materials, so that a vulnerability in a third-party library can be traced across device models.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction is toward continuous monitoring, automated vulnerability detection, and security requirements built into procurement and device design rather than bolted on later. More devices will carry unique identities and support over-the-air updates, while regulators push for software bills of materials and postmarket transparency. Hospital networks are likely to adopt zero trust segmentation and real-time anomaly detection tuned to clinical traffic. As connected devices incorporate more AI-driven features, security will also need to cover model inputs, telemetry integrity, and the risk that manipulated data changes clinical decisions.
